government.name: City of Burnaby
government.howBuilt: This list draws on the City of Burnaby's official candidate profiles, elector organization platforms, a Burnaby Heights Merchants Association mayoral questionnaire, and news coverage of the campaign, the 2026 budget, multiplex zoning changes, the Royal Oak supportive housing debate and Hastings Street bus lanes. We kept issues the City of Burnaby can act on through zoning, its budget, policing funding, streets, parks and council procedures. Matters mainly run by the province, such as hospital funding and schools, are left out.

issues.title: New housing in neighbourhoods
issues.description: How much multiplex and mid-size housing is allowed on residential streets, and how big new buildings can be.
issues.whatItAffects: Homeowners, renters, families looking for ground-oriented homes, and people living next to new buildings.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets zoning rules for building size, height, lot coverage and parking, within the minimums required by provincial housing law.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city handle multiplexes and mid-size housing in residential neighbourhoods?
viewQuestion.poleA: Allow more multiplexes and mid-size buildings across neighbourhoods
viewQuestion.poleB: Limit building size and require more parking to fit neighbourhood character

tradeoffs.context: Multiplex rules trade how many new homes can be built against how much existing streets change.

gains: More homes could be built on existing lots, adding supply
More families may find ground-oriented homes below detached-house prices
costs: Neighbours may see more height, shade and less on-street parking
Pipes, schools and roads may need upgrades sooner

gains: Streets may keep their current scale and look
Parking pressure on residential streets may be lower
costs: Fewer new homes may be built, keeping prices higher
Smaller allowable buildings may make some projects not worth building

issues.title: Property taxes and city spending
issues.description: How much property tax rises each year and how the city pays for big projects like new community centres.
issues.whatItAffects: Homeowners, renters through their rent, businesses, and everyone who uses city facilities and services.
issues.whoDecides: Council adopts the yearly financial plan, sets the tax rate and levies, and decides which capital projects go ahead.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city balance its budget?
viewQuestion.poleA: Freeze or cap tax increases, even if some projects wait
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep investing in facilities and services, even if taxes rise more

tradeoffs.context: Holding taxes down and keeping up a large building program pull on the same budget.

gains: Households and businesses would face smaller tax bills
Spending decisions may get closer review
costs: Some facilities, repairs or services may be delayed or trimmed
Reserves may be drawn down or costs pushed to future years

gains: New community centres and services could open on schedule
Infrastructure may be kept up before costs grow
costs: Tax bills could rise faster than inflation
Higher costs may be passed to renters and small businesses

issues.title: Community safety and policing
issues.description: How the city responds to crime, disorder and people in crisis, and how many officers and outreach workers it funds.
issues.whatItAffects: Residents, business owners, transit users, and people experiencing mental health or addiction crises.
issues.whoDecides: Council funds the Burnaby RCMP detachment and bylaw officers, and decides how much to spend on crisis-response and outreach programs.

viewQuestion.question: Where should more of the city's safety budget go?
viewQuestion.poleA: Hire more police officers and expand patrols and enforcement
viewQuestion.poleB: Expand crisis-response teams and outreach alongside police

tradeoffs.context: Safety budgets are limited, so more spending on officers often means less for outreach, and the reverse.

gains: More visible patrols may help people feel safer
Officers could respond faster to calls
costs: Policing costs may raise taxes or crowd out other services
Enforcement may move problems elsewhere rather than resolve them

gains: Trained workers could handle some mental-health calls that do not need police
Outreach may address addiction and crises behind some disorder
costs: Results may take longer to show and be harder to measure
Some residents may see less change in street conditions

issues.title: Shelters and supportive housing
issues.description: Where shelters and supportive housing for people leaving homelessness are located and what rules apply at those sites.
issues.whatItAffects: People who are unhoused, nearby residents and schools, and service providers.
issues.whoDecides: Council approves rezonings and city land for these sites, sets consultation requirements, and partners with BC Housing, which funds and operates most of them.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city handle new shelter and supportive housing sites?
viewQuestion.poleA: Keep approving sites so more people can move indoors
viewQuestion.poleB: Pause or limit new sites until stricter rules and more consultation

tradeoffs.context: Cities weigh adding shelter and supportive housing sites against responding to neighbourhood concerns about where they go.

gains: More people may move indoors and connect with services
Fewer people may need to sleep outside or in parks
costs: Nearby residents may worry about safety and disorder
Some sites may go ahead despite strong local opposition

gains: Neighbours may have more say and clearer rules at each site
Sites may open with more security and operating standards
costs: Fewer spaces may open, leaving more people unsheltered
Provincial funding may go to other cities if projects stall

issues.title: Affordable rental housing
issues.description: Whether and how the city builds below-market rental homes itself, through its Housing Authority and city-owned land.
issues.whatItAffects: Renters, lower- and middle-income households, seniors, and families priced out of the market.
issues.whoDecides: Council directs the Burnaby Housing Authority, decides how city land is used, and can speed approvals or waive fees for non-market housing.

viewQuestion.question: How directly should the city build affordable rental homes?
viewQuestion.poleA: Use city land and the Housing Authority to build many more non-market homes
viewQuestion.poleB: Rely more on private builders and senior-government funding, limiting city costs

tradeoffs.context: Direct city building can add affordable homes faster, but uses city land and money that could go elsewhere.

gains: More homes could rent below market rates
The city keeps long-term control over affordability
costs: City land and reserves are used that could serve other needs
The city takes on construction and operating risk

gains: City finances and land stay available for other uses
Private and senior-government partners carry more of the cost
costs: Fewer below-market homes may be built
Affordability may depend on outside funding decisions

issues.title: Transit, traffic and street space
issues.description: How busy streets like Hastings are shared among buses, bikes, pedestrians, drivers and curbside parking.
issues.whatItAffects: Transit riders, drivers, cyclists, pedestrians, and businesses that rely on street parking.
issues.whoDecides: Council controls city street design, parking and sidewalks, and approves bus lanes on city roads in partnership with TransLink.

viewQuestion.question: How should street space be shared on busy corridors?
viewQuestion.poleA: Add bus lanes, bike routes and sidewalks, even if parking is lost
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep curbside parking and general traffic lanes for drivers and shops

tradeoffs.context: Road space is fixed, so giving more to buses and bikes usually means less for parking and general traffic.

gains: Buses could run faster and more reliably
Walking and cycling may become safer
costs: Businesses may lose nearby customer parking
Some drivers may face slower trips or detours

gains: Shoppers and people with mobility needs keep convenient parking
Merchants may see less disruption
costs: Buses may stay slower in congested stretches
Fewer people may switch to transit, walking or cycling

issues.title: Council transparency and public input
issues.description: How council shares information and involves residents before making major decisions on projects and development.
issues.whatItAffects: Residents who want a say, neighbourhoods facing change, and the pace of city projects.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets its own meeting procedures, consultation practices and reporting to the public.

viewQuestion.question: How should council involve residents in decisions?
viewQuestion.poleA: Add town halls, question periods and longer consultation before decisions
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep current processes so decisions and projects move faster

tradeoffs.context: More consultation gives residents more say but adds time and cost to decisions.

gains: Residents may have more chances to be heard
Decisions may be easier for the public to understand
costs: Projects and housing approvals may take longer
Meetings and outreach add staff costs

gains: Projects and approvals may move faster
Staff time stays focused on delivering services
costs: Some residents may feel left out of decisions
Concerns may surface later, after plans are set

issues.title: Parks, trees and green space
issues.description: How much parkland and tree cover the city keeps and adds as it grows.
issues.whatItAffects: Residents who use parks and trails, wildlife habitat, and land available for other uses.
issues.whoDecides: Council buys and zones parkland, sets tree-protection rules, and funds park maintenance and upgrades.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city protect parks and trees as it grows?
viewQuestion.poleA: Buy more parkland and require tree protection, even if it adds costs
viewQuestion.poleB: Focus on maintaining existing parks, keeping land and money for other needs

tradeoffs.context: Adding parkland and protecting trees competes with land for housing and with other spending.

gains: More residents could live near a park
Tree cover may help with heat and habitat
costs: Buying land adds cost to the city budget
Tree rules may add cost or limits to some projects

gains: Money can go to upkeep of parks people already use
More land may stay available for housing and facilities
costs: Fast-growing areas may have less green space per person
Tree cover may grow more slowly

locations: Six advance voting locations across Burnaby; see the City's voting locations map at https://gis.burnaby.ca/electionvotinglocations/

election.howToVote: Burnaby voters can vote at any of 33 voting places on General Voting Day (Saturday, Oct. 17, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.) or at six advance voting locations on Oct. 3, 7 or 10. Voters who are not already registered can register at the voting place with two pieces of ID that together prove identity and residential address, one with a signature. Non-resident property electors should contact the Burnaby Election Office.
election.voteByMail: All eligible voters could apply to vote by mail from Aug. 31 to Oct. 5; completed ballots must be received by 8 p.m. on Oct. 17, by mail, at a drop box, or at any voting place.

electorOrganizations.name: BCA - Burnaby Citizens Association
electorOrganizations.blurb: Describes itself as founded in 1955 to act on issues that matter to residents, with a focus on progressive local governance and the well-being of all citizens.

electorOrganizations.name: Burnaby First
electorOrganizations.blurb: Describes itself as advocating accountability on operating costs, property tax, public safety and green spaces.

electorOrganizations.name: Burnaby Green Party
electorOrganizations.blurb: Presents a platform centred on non-market housing, faster transit, cycling and sidewalks, climate resilience, and published progress targets.

electorOrganizations.name: New Burnaby Party
electorOrganizations.blurb: Says its platform comes from consultations with residents and covers eight areas, including public safety, taxes, parks and council independence.

electorOrganizations.name: Restore Burnaby Alliance
electorOrganizations.blurb: Describes its focus as accountability, affordability, financial responsibility and public safety, under the tagline Restore, Renew, Rebuild, Together.
